title: The Particle Zoo
description: Quarks, leptons, and the fundamental constituents of matter

concepts.title: Three Generations of Matter
concepts.contentHtml:
All ordinary matter is built from twelve fermions arranged in three generations. Each generation has two quarks and two leptons.

Generation 1: up and down quarks (which build protons and neutrons), the electron, and the electron neutrino. Everyday matter uses only this generation.

Generations 2 and 3 (charm/strange/muon/μ-neutrino, top/bottom/tau/τ-neutrino) are heavier copies that exist only briefly in cosmic rays and accelerators. Why three generations? Nobody knows.

concepts.title: Quarks Are Confined
concepts.contentHtml:
You can't extract a single quark. The strong force between them grows stronger with distance — pull two quarks apart and you put so much energy into the bond that you make new quark-antiquark pairs out of vacuum.

So quarks always come in colorless combinations: baryons (three quarks, like protons = uud and neutrons = udd) or mesons (quark + antiquark, like pions).

This 'confinement' is a property of QCD that has resisted analytical proof — it's one of the Millennium Prize Problems.

concepts.title: Antimatter
concepts.contentHtml:
Every fermion has an antiparticle with the same mass but opposite charge and quantum numbers. Anti-electrons (positrons), antiquarks, antiprotons.

Dirac predicted antimatter from his relativistic equation in 1928; positrons were found in 1932. Today, PET scans use positron-electron annihilation routinely.

The universe contains far more matter than antimatter, and we don't fully know why. This baryogenesis problem is one of the deepest open questions in cosmology.

title: The Four Forces
description: Strong, weak, electromagnetic, gravity — and the bosons that carry them

concepts.title: Force-Carrying Bosons
concepts.contentHtml:
In the Standard Model, forces are mediated by exchange particles called gauge bosons:

• Electromagnetism — photon (γ), massless, infinite range
• Strong force — eight gluons, massless, but confined to nuclear distances
• Weak force — W⁺, W⁻, Z⁰ bosons; very heavy, so very short range
• Gravity — hypothetical graviton; not part of the Standard Model

concepts.title: Why the Weak Force Is Weak
concepts.contentHtml:
The weak force isn't intrinsically feeble — its coupling is comparable to electromagnetism's. It's short-ranged because its mediators (W and Z) are about 100 times the proton mass.

Heavy mediators die off exponentially with distance — beyond a fraction of an attometer, weak interactions are essentially impossible. So fusion in the Sun (which needs a weak interaction to convert protons to neutrons) is bottlenecked, and that's why stars burn slowly enough for life to evolve.

concepts.title: Quantum Chromodynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
QCD is the theory of the strong force. Quarks carry one of three 'color charges' (red, green, blue — names; nothing to do with visual color). Gluons carry combinations of color and anticolor.

Unlike photons, gluons interact with each other — that self-interaction is why the force grows stronger at long distances and weaker at short distances (asymptotic freedom, Nobel 2004).

concepts.title: The Higgs Field
concepts.contentHtml:
The Standard Model's gauge symmetry would naively force every elementary particle to be massless. But quarks, leptons, and W/Z bosons are clearly not.

The fix: a scalar field — the Higgs field — that fills all of space with a non-zero value. Other particles 'drag' through it, gaining effective mass proportional to how strongly they couple to it.

The top quark has a strong Higgs coupling and a mass of 173 GeV. The electron's coupling is tiny — only 0.5 MeV.

concepts.title: Discovering the Higgs
concepts.contentHtml:
Predicted by Higgs, Englert, Brout and others in 1964, the Higgs boson — an excitation of the field — was finally observed at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012.

Its mass: about 125 GeV. The discovery completed the Standard Model and earned the 2013 Nobel for Higgs and Englert.

The LHC produces Higgs bosons at a rate of roughly one per second of running — but only a few decay channels are clean enough to spot above the background.

concepts.title: Most Mass Is Not From the Higgs
concepts.contentHtml:
The proton's mass is about 938 MeV. The masses of its three constituent quarks add up to only about 10 MeV.

The other 99% comes from QCD binding energy — the gluon field and the kinetic energy of confined quarks (E = mc²). Almost all the mass of ordinary matter is field energy, not Higgs mass.

So the Higgs gives mass to the elementary fermions and W/Z bosons; QCD gives mass to composite hadrons. Both stories are essential.

concepts.title: Why High Energy?
concepts.contentHtml:
To create a heavy particle of mass M, you need at least Mc² of energy — relativistic mass-energy equivalence in action.

To probe small distances, you need short wavelengths: λ = h/p. High momentum means small wavelength means resolution of fine structure inside, say, a proton.

Both push us toward ever-higher energies. The LHC collides protons at 13 TeV — the highest energies ever produced in a controlled environment.

concepts.title: Inside the LHC
concepts.contentHtml:
The Large Hadron Collider is a 27-km ring at CERN where two counter-rotating proton beams reach 99.9999991% of the speed of light, then collide head-on.

Superconducting magnets at 1.9 K (colder than space) bend the beams. Each detector — ATLAS, CMS — is the size of a cathedral and contains millions of channels of electronics.

Roughly 40 million collisions per second occur in each detector, generating petabytes of data. Triggers cut this to a manageable rate before reconstruction.

concepts.title: Detecting Particles
concepts.contentHtml:
You can't see a quark. You see what its decay products do.

Layers of a typical detector: tracker (silicon, records charged particle paths), electromagnetic calorimeter (electrons and photons deposit energy here), hadronic calorimeter (protons, pions, neutrons), muon chambers on the outside (only muons make it that far).

Neutrinos escape — their presence is inferred from missing momentum. Reconstructing an event is a careful jigsaw puzzle.

title: Beyond the Standard Model
description: Open questions and what comes next

concepts.title: What the Standard Model Cannot Explain
concepts.contentHtml:
The Standard Model is staggeringly accurate — the electron's magnetic moment matches theory to 12 decimal places. But it leaves big gaps:

• Dark matter — astrophysics demands it; SM has no candidate.
• Gravity — not part of the SM at all.
• Neutrino masses — observed (oscillations), but the mechanism is unclear.
• Matter-antimatter asymmetry — universe is matter-dominated; SM CP-violation is too small to explain it.
• Hierarchy problem — why is the Higgs mass not driven up to the Planck scale by quantum corrections?

concepts.title: Supersymmetry, Dark Matter, & WIMPs
concepts.contentHtml:
Supersymmetry (SUSY) proposes a partner for every Standard Model particle, with spin differing by ½. The lightest SUSY particle could be a stable, weakly-interacting massive particle (a 'WIMP') — a natural dark matter candidate.

SUSY would also stabilize the Higgs mass. But despite years of LHC searches, no SUSY particles have been found at accessible energies. Theorists are revising or abandoning the simplest versions.

Direct dark matter searches (XENON, LUX) and indirect detection continue. The truth remains unsettled.

concepts.title: Toward Unification
concepts.contentHtml:
Electromagnetism and the weak force are already unified into one electroweak theory. Some Grand Unified Theories (GUTs) predict that the strong force joins them at energies near 10¹⁶ GeV.

Strings and quantum gravity propose to unify everything, including gravity. Direct experimental tests at unification scales are far beyond reach — but cosmology, neutrino experiments, and rare decays offer indirect probes.

Particle physics is in an interesting moment: we have a theory that works incredibly well, and clear evidence that it can't be the whole story.
